project_and_compatibility.implementation_language: Cypress App is primarily implemented in TypeScript and JavaScript. Tests, support code, plugins, and configuration can be authored in TypeScript or JavaScript and run with the Cypress binary plus a supported Node.js runtime. [S1][S2][S8]
project_and_compatibility.node_and_typescript_compatibility: Verified for this repository's target stack. Cypress 15.21.0 declares Node.js ^20.1.0, ^22.0.0, or >=24.0.0 and the official documentation supports npm >=10.1.0. Cypress 15.14.0 added TypeScript 6.0 support; current documentation supports TypeScript 5.x, 6.x, and 7.x. A separate cypress/tsconfig.json is advisable so Cypress's global Mocha, Chai, and jQuery types do not pollute the Parcel application's ESNext/bundler tsconfig. Cypress configuration supports .ts, .mts, and .cts with Node module rules, so the repository may retain its current package.json without a type field and use cypress.config.ts as CommonJS, or use cypress.config.mts for explicit ESM. [S1][S2][S8][S21]
project_and_compatibility.operating_system_support: Official support includes Linux x64 and arm64 on Ubuntu >=22.04, Debian >=11, and Fedora >=43. GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners fit this support window. Native installation requires GTK, GBM, NSS, X11/Xvfb, audio, and related libraries; official Debian-based Cypress Docker images supply them. On arm64, official browser-image availability is narrower: Chrome is available only from version 151, Firefox from 136, and Edge is unavailable. [S1][S9]
project_and_compatibility.license_and_governance: The Cypress App repository and npm package use the permissive MIT License and are owned and led by Cypress.io. Development occurs publicly in cypress-io/cypress, while Cypress.io commercially stewards the optional proprietary Cypress Cloud service. The license permits private, commercial, modified, and redistributed repository use subject to preserving the license notice. This is company-led open source rather than neutral-foundation governance. [S8][S19][S20]
project_and_compatibility.installation_model: Install cypress as a dev dependency with npm install --save-dev cypress. Its postinstall downloads a platform-specific Cypress binary into a global cache, normally ~/.cache/Cypress on Linux; npx cypress install can perform that step explicitly. Electron is bundled in Cypress 15, while Chrome, Edge, and Firefox are system-installed, GitHub-runner-provided, or supplied through cypress/browsers images. Experimental WebKit additionally requires playwright-webkit and Linux WebKit dependencies. Official cypress/base, cypress/browsers, cypress/included, and cypress/factory images support pinned environments. [S1][S3][S9]
project_and_compatibility.candidate_scope_and_layer: Complete end-to-end browser testing framework: integrated Mocha-based runner, assertions, browser launcher, command log, retry model, network proxy/interception, fixtures, screenshots, videos, reporters, plugin/node-event API, and interactive authoring application. It is not merely a browser driver or an abstraction over another runner. [S11][S12][S13][S14][S15]
project_and_compatibility.authoring_and_async_model: Tests use Cypress's framework-specific command queue and Chainable DSL, for example cy.get(...).should(...), rather than native async/await for browser commands. Commands enqueue asynchronously; queries and assertions retry, while actions execute once after actionability checks. Values are consumed through .then(), aliases, or cy.wrap(). Ordinary promises can be used in hooks and Node tasks, but mixing them with queued commands requires care. This model is productive but creates meaningful Cypress lock-in and a learning boundary for developers expecting Promise-returning browser APIs. [S12]
project_and_compatibility.build_pipeline_coupling: E2E tests can black-box the existing application with baseUrl and cy.visit() and do not require Cypress to transform the Parcel source, substitute Vite, or instrument the production bundle. The production build can be served by the Gin container on port 80; development can use Parcel on port 8000 with the existing /api proxy to Gin on port 8080. Cypress separately preprocesses test/configuration TypeScript with its own tooling, so a dedicated Cypress tsconfig avoids coupling that test compilation to the application's TypeScript configuration. [S2][S21]
project_and_compatibility.testability_instrumentation_required: No special application route, injected script, relaxed CORS rule, or alternate build is mandatory for basic E2E operation. Reliable suites would benefit from adding stable data-cy attributes to high-value controls because the current templates primarily expose dynamic IDs, visible labels, and ARIA labels; Cypress explicitly recommends dedicated data attributes. Test-only database reset/seeding through an authenticated test API or a cy.task Node handler is also advisable. These are testability improvements, not Cypress runtime requirements. Cypress proxies and rewrites application traffic internally, so unusually strict CSP or SRI may require Cypress configuration, but no such project constraint was identified. [S13][S21]

Cypress's site lists enterprise users, but those vendor claims are supporting rather than independent evidence. [S9][S10][S15][S16][S17][S24]

Public GitHub issues and discussions, Discord, learning material, videos, and a large body of community plugins and third-party answers provide multiple support paths. Free users receive community support; paid Cloud tiers add email or premium support. [S1][S10][S12][S15][S24]

This supports stable-to-slightly-growing use, but one year-over-year week is sensitive to CI caching, bots, transitive installs, and calendar effects; it is insufficient to establish a durable trend by itself. [S7]
community_adoption.adoption_metric_normalization: The primary registry metric is direct downloads of npm package cypress, not all Cypress plugins, Docker pulls, Cloud users, or unique projects, over the explicitly fixed 2026-08-14 to 2026-08-20 window. Repeated CI installs and cache misses can count multiple times, while cached binaries can reduce downloads. The package includes E2E and component-testing capabilities, so downloads cannot be attributed solely to E2E. Stars and forks are cumulative interest signals, not current production usage. The vendor's 1.5M+ dependent-repository claim is rounded and may include direct and transitive package relationships. [S6][S7][S8][S24]

browser_and_runtime_coverage.browser_engines: Stable support covers Chromium-family browsers through bundled Electron 15.x, installed Chrome/Chrome for Testing/Chromium, and Microsoft Edge, plus installed Firefox. Cypress officially supports the latest three major Chrome, Edge, and Firefox versions. WebKit is experimental, requires experimentalWebKitSupport plus playwright-webkit, and has documented gaps including no cy.origin(), no Test Replay, disabled forceNetworkError, and input/stack/video limitations. Native Safari and mobile browsers are not controlled. [S1][S3]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.browser_protocol: Cypress uses a framework-specific architecture combining code in the browser, a local Node process, and an HTTP proxy. Chromium launch/control uses Chrome DevTools Protocol; current Firefox automation uses WebDriver BiDi and geckodriver for launch, with Firefox >=140 required; experimental WebKit is launched through Playwright's WebKit integration. The mixed implementation enables network rewriting and time-travel UX but is not a portable WebDriver client and inherits browser-specific constraints. [S3][S13]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.headless_and_headed_modes: cypress run is headless by default for Electron, Chrome-family, Firefox, and experimental WebKit and accepts --headed for visible execution. cypress open is always headed and provides the interactive runner. Headless Chrome uses the modern headless implementation; headless Linux is supported directly or through Xvfb where required. [S3][S9]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.browser_version_management: Each Cypress 15 release bundles a fixed Electron/Chromium runtime. Cypress detects installed Chrome-family and Firefox browsers; Chrome for Testing or long-form cypress/browsers image tags can pin exact versions and avoid auto-update drift. Official images pin Node and browser combinations. Firefox may download the latest geckodriver through its wrapper when no cached driver exists, creating an air-gapped/network and possible drift concern unless a current image or explicit cache/path is used. Experimental WebKit version follows the installed playwright-webkit package. [S3][S9]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.parallel_browser_support: One Cypress process selects one browser per invocation; Cypress has no Playwright-style projects array that runs a browser matrix in one command. Run separate CI matrix jobs for Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Electron, or WebKit. Specs run sequentially in one Cypress process; multi-machine spec distribution with --parallel and dynamic load balancing requires recording to Cypress Cloud, while fully local parallelism requires explicit spec partitioning or community/custom tooling. [S9][S10]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.mobile_emulation: cy.viewport() supports explicit dimensions, orientation, and named phone/tablet viewport presets, and configuration can override userAgent. This is responsive-layout simulation, not full device emulation: devicePixelRatio is not simulated, and Cypress does not provide a unified core device profile covering touch hardware, sensors, locale, timezone, network, and mobile browser binaries. Real iOS Safari and Android Chrome require external infrastructure rather than core Cypress. [S25]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.real_browser_fidelity: Installed Chrome, Chromium, Edge, and Firefox runs use real desktop browser binaries in Cypress-controlled isolated profiles. Bundled Electron is Chromium-based but is not an end-user browser, and Cypress recommends another browser for representative coverage. Experimental WebKit uses Playwright's WebKit build; it is not Apple's Safari application and cannot validate Safari-only UI chrome, Apple platform integration, codecs, keychain, or OS rendering. Viewport presets likewise do not equal physical mobile-device testing. [S3][S25]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.environment_determinism_controls: Core controls include cy.clock()/cy.tick() for Date and browser timers, fixed viewport dimensions/orientation, isolated browser profiles, browser launch flags/preferences, network stubs/delays/errors, fixed fixtures, and screenshot animation handling. Headless runs default to 1280x720 screen and DPR 1, while the AUT viewport defaults to 1000x660 unless configured. Locale, timezone, geolocation, permissions, DPR, reduced motion, and randomness lack one unified cross-browser device/project profile and generally require environment variables, browser launch arguments, stubs, CSS, or application-level setup. cy.clock() affects only the top window, not embedded iframes. [S3][S13][S25][S26]

application_fit.dynamic_dom_synchronization: Good fit for HTMX swaps and asynchronous Handlebars rendering when tests use fresh query chains and observable end states. Cypress retries linked DOM queries/assertions and re-runs queries before an action until actionability passes; cy.intercept aliases can explicitly await HTMX XHR/fetch responses. Because a passed mid-chain assertion locks its subject, an HTMX replacement can still produce a detached element for later chained queries. Split chains and re-query after actions/swaps rather than retaining jQuery elements or using non-retried .then() callbacks. [S12][S13][S21]
application_fit.routing_support: Navigo history/path routing can be exercised through links and browser actions, while retrying cy.location('pathname'), cy.url(), and cy.go() assertions verify route transitions. Direct deep links work if the independently served application returns root.html or the intended route fallback; this must be verified for the Gin production server. Test isolation visits about:blank before each test, so each test should visit its route and not depend on prior route state. [S21][S27]
application_fit.locator_model: Core Cypress offers CSS selectors through cy.get(), scoped queries, visible-text matching through cy.contains(), and custom queries. Accessible role/name locators require the maintained community Cypress Testing Library plugin rather than a core locator API. Core queries are not globally strict: they can yield collections, although many actions reject multiple targets unless configured. The project has useful IDs and ARIA labels but no observed data-cy attributes. Stable data-cy selectors are Cypress's recommendation. Fresh query chains reacquire HTMX-replaced elements; aliases of DOM queries can re-run, but captured raw elements and subjects after assertion boundaries can become stale. [S12][S17][S21]
application_fit.form_interaction: Cypress supports focus, blur, clear, type, select, check, uncheck, submit, native Tab through cy.press(), and assertions on values, validity, attributes, and focused elements. Separate cy.get() calls between focus/type/blur actions are recommended when application handlers can replace a row. This can cover the repository's input masks, hidden-value synchronization, dynamic allocation rows, Bootstrap validation classes, and native validity APIs. Input events are browser-dispatched by Cypress rather than operating-system-level keystrokes; WebKit documents additional type-event differences. [S3][S12][S17][S21]
application_fit.canvas_and_download_support: Chart.js canvases can be validated without relying only on pixels by asserting canvas size/presence, reading the 2D context or toDataURL(), exposing/inspecting the Chart instance or its application data, and checking accessible/table equivalents; Cypress visual plugins can add pixel baselines for a small stable set. Browser downloads are redirected to cypress/downloads without a native Save As prompt and can be checked with cy.readFile() or cy.task(). Cypress does not provide built-in screenshot comparison, and project code may need to expose chart semantic state if it is not otherwise reachable. [S3][S16][S21]
application_fit.network_and_api_access: Strong fit. cy.request() can seed/query REST endpoints without the UI, while cy.intercept() observes, aliases, mutates, delays, fails, or fixtures XHR/fetch requests. Interception can let the Gin API run normally while replacing only Yahoo Finance-bound browser traffic if that traffic originates in the browser. If Yahoo Finance is called exclusively by the Go backend, browser interception cannot see it; use backend dependency injection, a fake upstream endpoint, or seeded API/database state. Request and response bodies, headers, methods, URLs, and statuses are assertable. [S13][S21]
application_fit.same_origin_support: The consolidated production server exposes the application and /api from one origin at localhost:80, and Parcel's development server exposes localhost:8000 while proxying /api to localhost:8080. Cypress baseUrl can target either public origin with relative visits and requests, so no CORS change is needed. Cross-origin restrictions and cy.origin() are not involved in these normal paths. [S13][S21]
application_fit.test_isolation: Cypress clears the page, cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage, aliases, clocks, intercepts, spies, stubs, and viewport changes before each E2E test when testIsolation is enabled. It does not create a new OS process or independent browser context per test, and IndexedDB or other storage must be cleared manually. PostgreSQL is external to browser isolation; reliable parallel suites need a reset/seed API or cy.task plus unique test namespaces, transactions, schemas, databases, or serialized DB-mutating specs. [S18]
application_fit.external_server_model: Supported and conventional. Set e2e.baseUrl or CYPRESS_BASE_URL and run tests against any independently started Gin/Parcel/Docker Compose application. Cypress verifies baseUrl availability for visits but expects the server to be started outside test code. Different local and CI ports can be selected through configuration/environment overrides. [S9][S21]
application_fit.application_lifecycle: Cypress itself does not provide a declarative multi-service webServer lifecycle. The official GitHub Action has build, start, and wait-on options, and start-server-and-test or custom Node orchestration can start one or more commands. This repository needs custom CI steps to build the Parcel/Gin image, create disposable PostgreSQL storage, run Docker Compose, wait for database health, Flyway completion and HTTP/API readiness, execute Cypress, capture service logs, and docker compose down --volumes under an always-run cleanup step. Existing Compose dependency conditions help, but start.sh persists data under the home directory and stop.sh stops rather than removes services/volumes, so they are not sufficient as an isolated CI harness. [S9][S10][S21]
application_fit.visual_regression_workflow: Cypress core captures screenshots but does not compare them. Official documentation lists actively maintained open-source image-diff plugins and commercial services. An open-source project workflow must own baseline files, approval review, masking/threshold configuration, per-browser baselines, and CI diff uploads. Pin the browser/OS/fonts in a Cypress Docker image, fix viewport/time/data, disable animations, and wait for Chart.js completion. Chart canvases are visually testable, but semantic dataset assertions should remain primary to reduce pixel flake. [S14][S16]
application_fit.accessibility_audit_integration: Compatible through the community cypress-axe plugin using axe-core, with other open-source reporters/plugins available. Cypress Testing Library can add role/label locators, and cy.press() supports native Tab-focused keyboard tests. Core Cypress does not supply ARIA snapshot assertions. Cypress Accessibility performs automatic step-level analysis in Cloud but is a paid premium solution; it is unnecessary for basic open-source axe scans and explicit semantic/keyboard assertions. [S17]

reliability.waiting_model: Linked queries and assertions retry from the top until their timeout; action commands re-run preceding queries and wait for existence, visibility, enablement, coverage, stability, and scroll/actionability before acting once. cy.visit() waits for page load, cy.location()/cy.url() poll SPA state, and cy.intercept()+cy.wait('@alias') provides explicit request/response synchronization. Non-query actions, .then() callbacks, and assertions chained directly to some yielded one-shot values are not automatically replayed, so tests must respect retry boundaries. [S12][S13][S27]
reliability.flake_controls: Configurable retries exist globally, separately for run/open mode, and per suite/test; default is zero. Every retry reruns beforeEach/afterEach and creates attempt-specific failure screenshots. Experimental retry strategies can require passes and classify flake. Timeouts are scoped per command/configuration, deterministic waits can use network aliases or state assertions, and fixed sleeps are discouraged. Cypress lacks a core repeat-each stress flag and automatic quarantine in the local runner; repeat loops and quarantine policy require CI/custom tooling or Cloud features. [S11][S12]
reliability.isolation_model: Default E2E isolation resets the page and common browser storage before each test, but one runner process does not provide Playwright-style independent browser contexts. IndexedDB persists unless explicitly deleted. Suites may opt out at describe level for serial scenarios, but this increases order dependence. Database state is never reset by Cypress, so serial DB scenarios should be deliberately grouped while independent tests reset or namespace server state. [S18]
reliability.resource_usage: [uncertain] Official guidance recommends at least 2 CPUs and 4 GB RAM in CI, with 8 GB or more for long runs or video; the Real World App uses larger runners. Each parallel shard is a Cypress process plus a browser and Xvfb where applicable. Video and compression add CPU, memory, disk, and post-processing time. The npm package metadata reports 4.68 MB unpacked JavaScript package content, but the separately downloaded Cypress binary and browser images are much larger. No benchmark was run against this repository, so execution time, peak memory, binary size, and safe shard density remain unmeasured. [S1][S8][S9]
reliability.parallelism_controls: The safest initial configuration is one DB-mutating Cypress invocation and one browser, with spec-level serialization. Later, GitHub matrices can split read-only specs or use isolated PostgreSQL databases/schemas per job. Cypress Cloud can dynamically load-balance whole specs across machines but cannot make shared database writes safe; explicit groups, separate base URLs/data namespaces, and CI concurrency limits remain necessary. Without Cloud, assign disjoint --spec globs to jobs or use a maintained splitter and merge reports explicitly. [S9][S10]
reliability.flake_observability: The open runner shows retry attempts and preserves attempt-specific screenshots; videos can include every attempt, and JUnit/JSON-capable community reporters can expose attempt results for CI processing. It does not provide a built-in local historical flake database, quarantine workflow, trend dashboard, or replay trace. Cypress Cloud adds flaky badges, flake rate/history, alerts, Test Replay, analytics, and test-level rerun features, with some flake analytics requiring paid tiers. A service-free solution must ingest reporter output and retain artifacts/history itself. [S11][S15][S24]

diagnostics_and_developer_experience.failure_artifacts: Core local artifacts include automatic failure screenshots in cypress run, manual screenshots, optional per-spec MP4 video, CLI stack/error output, and reporter files. Interactive Command Log snapshots show DOM state and XHR/fetch routes. Cypress does not create a portable local execution trace, HAR, or complete browser-console/network archive comparable to a trace viewer; console capture and durable network logs need event hooks/plugins. Cypress Cloud adds Test Replay with DOM, network, console, JavaScript errors, and rendering context. [S13][S14][S15]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.debugging_tools: cypress open provides a headed interactive runner, live Command Log, DOM snapshots/time travel, browser DevTools console output, reruns, .pause(), .debug(), and selector inspection. cypress run supports --headed and --no-exit for reproduction. IDE type declarations/JSDoc and source maps improve navigation. Cloud Test Replay supplies remote time travel but is optional. [S2][S12][S14]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.test_generation: Cypress Studio records click, type, check, uncheck, and select interactions, generates selectors, supports manual assertions, and edits test source. Non-AI Studio does not require a Cloud account, but current documentation says it requires internet access and source maps. Studio AI is opt-in, Cloud-connected, beta functionality that proposes assertions. Generated selector quality follows a priority headed by data-cy/data-test/data-testid, then progressively more fragile attributes, so generated code still requires review. [S23]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.reporters: The built-in default spec reporter writes to stdout; JUnit and TeamCity are bundled, and any compatible Mocha reporter can be installed, including JSON/HTML options such as Mochawesome. Multiple reporters require a package such as cypress-multi-reporters. Every spec is processed separately, so report filenames need a hash and JUnit/Mochawesome outputs need an explicit merge step. GitHub annotations can be produced through suitable reporters or workflow processing; Cloud provides its own hosted reports. [S15]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.documentation_quality: High breadth and currentness. Official pages separately document installation, TypeScript, command semantics, browser limits, CI, retries, isolation, networking, artifacts, accessibility, visual testing, security, migrations, changelogs, and common failure modes, often with JavaScript and TypeScript examples. Several pages used here were updated in July or August 2026. The documentation also states important limitations, including experimental WebKit, non-cleared IndexedDB, non-strict retry boundaries, and Cloud-only features. [S1][S2][S3][S9][S12][S18]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.local_workflow: Use npx cypress open for browser selection, spec selection, interactive reruns, time travel, Studio, and DevTools. Use npx cypress run --spec <glob> --browser chrome for a focused CI-like run, optionally --headed --no-exit to retain the final state. Separate runMode/openMode retries avoid hiding failures during authoring. The repository must first start its Gin/Parcel/Compose services; Cypress should not start them from inside a test. [S3][S9][S11][S23]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.failure_log_correlation: Cypress timestamps and orders browser commands, request aliases, errors, screenshots, and videos, but it does not automatically ingest Gin, PostgreSQL, Flyway, or Docker Compose logs into one local timeline. The workflow should record test start/end times, stream service logs to separate files, label cy.intercept aliases, capture browser uncaught exceptions/console messages, and upload compose ps/logs plus Flyway output on failure. Cloud Replay correlates browser-side evidence only; backend correlation remains custom. [S9][S13][S21]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.artifact_data_exposure: Screenshots, video, HTML/JSON/JUnit reports, Command Log snapshots, network bodies, console output, downloads, and Cloud Test Replay can expose portfolio values, credentials, API responses, or tokens. cy.env() hides values only while retrieving them; later assertions/logs can print them. Use synthetic data, Cypress/GitHub secrets, {log:false} for sensitive commands/intercepts, screenshot blackout where practical, selective artifact retention, private CI artifacts, and no storage-state dumps. Cloud uploads test content to US multi-tenant storage; public projects make content public. No universal automatic redaction for all local artifacts was identified. [S14][S20][S28]

github_actions_fit.official_ci_support: Strong. Cypress maintains cypress-io/github-action, with v7 recommended and v7.4.3 released 2026-08-20. Official documentation targets ubuntu-24.04 and covers dependency installation, start/wait, browser selection, caching, matrices, Cloud recording, and Docker images. GitHub-hosted Ubuntu includes supported browsers, while official images offer pinning. [S10][S22]
github_actions_fit.browser_caching: The official action automatically caches/restores package-manager and Cypress dependencies. For manual workflows, cache the package-manager cache and ~/.cache/Cypress after npm ci; do not cache node_modules. Use strict cache keys to avoid accumulating old Cypress binaries. Long-form Docker tags avoid runtime browser download but shift caching to container layers. Firefox driver downloads should also be made deterministic through a current image/cache for offline CI. [S9][S10]
github_actions_fit.artifact_integration: Straightforward but not automatic: use actions/upload-artifact with if: always() for cypress/screenshots, cypress/videos, JUnit/Mochawesome output, downloads as appropriate, and collected application/Compose logs. Configure screenshot/video retention and compression to control size. Cypress Cloud can host screenshots, videos, Test Replay, and reports when --record is used, but local GitHub artifacts remain sufficient for core OSS execution. [S10][S14][S15]
github_actions_fit.sharding_and_matrix_support: GitHub matrix jobs can cover browsers, viewports, and manually assigned spec partitions. Native Cypress --parallel dynamic spec balancing, run grouping, merged hosted results, and balancing require Cypress Cloud recording. Service-free sharding needs fixed --spec partitions or community tooling and explicit JUnit/Mochawesome merge jobs. Retry attempts occur within the worker that owns a spec; rerunning a failed GitHub job is separate from Cypress test retries. Browser versions must match across Cloud parallel workers, so pinned Docker images are recommended. [S10][S15]
github_actions_fit.container_compatibility: Cypress runs well on Ubuntu hosts or in official Debian containers. This repository itself needs Docker Compose for Gin, PostgreSQL, and Flyway. The least complex GitHub setup is to run Cypress directly on the Ubuntu host, start Compose on the same host, and browse exposed localhost ports. Running the whole job inside cypress/browsers complicates access to the host Docker daemon and sibling Compose networking unless the workflow deliberately mounts/configures Docker. Pin Chrome for Testing or an image where reproducibility outweighs that complexity. [S9][S10][S21]
github_actions_fit.failure_cleanup: Cypress normally closes its browser/Xvfb process, but repository services and data volumes require explicit cleanup. Add an if: always() step that captures docker compose ps/logs and runs docker compose down --volumes --remove-orphans, and use job-level timeouts/concurrency cancellation. Use disposable workspace-owned PostgreSQL storage rather than start.sh's persistent home-directory path. GitHub cancellation can interrupt ordinary commands, so cleanup should be idempotent and the next run should remove stale project-scoped resources before startup. [S9][S21]

cost_and_risk.open_source_completeness: All capabilities required to author and execute deterministic local/CI E2E tests are available under MIT or compatible open-source tooling: runner, Chrome/Firefox control, network interception, API calls, retries, screenshots, videos, JUnit, Docker images, axe-core integration, and community visual diffing. Stable WebKit is not available, and advanced orchestration/observability are not open-source core capabilities. [S14][S15][S16][S17][S19]
cost_and_risk.optional_cloud_dependency: No Cloud account is required for ordinary tests, retries, screenshots, local videos, network control, reports, or open mode. Cypress Cloud is required for Cypress's native --parallel load balancing and supplies hosted Test Replay, retained runs/artifacts, analytics, integration comments/statuses, flake management, prioritization, cancellation, UI Coverage, Accessibility, and AI features according to tier. The free plan listed 500 recorded results/month; Team started at USD 799/year on 2026-08-22. Equivalent local pieces exist for artifacts, reports, fixed sharding, axe, and visual diffs, but no equally integrated core local replay/analytics service is bundled. [S9][S10][S17][S24]
cost_and_risk.migration_cost: Moderate to high for a mature suite. Test intent, CSS/data selectors, fixtures, and API concepts are portable, but cy.* command queues, Chainable custom commands, aliases, retry semantics, cy.intercept, Node events/tasks, Cypress configuration, Studio output, and Cloud run metadata are framework-specific. Moving to native async/await frameworks requires structural rewrites rather than mechanical import changes. Avoid overusing custom commands and Cloud-only control flow to limit lock-in. [S12][S13][S15]
cost_and_risk.security_and_supply_chain: The npm package is signed, publishes integrity hashes, and release 15.21 includes a downloadable SBOM artifact. The MIT source, public changelog, SECURITY.md disclosure route, frequent dependency upgrades, and recent CVE-driven tar/esbuild/undici updates are positive. Risks include a broad dependency tree, a postinstall binary download, optional geckodriver download, official Docker-image trust, privileged browser/proxy behavior, and optional telemetry/Cloud egress. Pin package/image versions and lockfiles, cache verified binaries, scan dependencies/images/SBOMs, use CYPRESS_DISABLE_GUEST_TELEMETRY where required, and keep secrets out of bundled specs and artifacts. [S4][S5][S8][S20]
cost_and_risk.custom_harness_burden: Moderate. Cypress supplies browser/network/test lifecycle but the repository must add Cypress configuration/specs, stable selectors, REST/database fixtures, a PostgreSQL reset or namespace strategy, Yahoo Finance replacement at the correct backend boundary, Compose/Flyway readiness, deterministic ports, log collection, report/artifact upload, and cleanup. The official action reduces Node/cache/start-wait work, but the multi-service disposable environment and backend external-service seam remain project-owned. [S9][S10][S13][S21]
cost_and_risk.capability_delivery_tier: Core OSS: E2E runner, TypeScript, Chrome/Edge/Firefox/Electron 15, headless/headed mode, command retries, optional test retries, test isolation, cy.request, cy.intercept, screenshots, video, downloads, spec/JUnit reporters, and open mode. Experimental core plus external package: WebKit via playwright-webkit. Official OSS companion: GitHub Action and Docker images. Community OSS: Testing Library accessible locators, cypress-axe, visual image diffing, richer/multiple reporters, and fixed sharding helpers. Custom project code: Docker Compose/Flyway readiness, DB reset, backend Yahoo stub, service-log correlation, deterministic cleanup, and semantic Chart.js assertions. Cloud/free-or-paid SaaS: smart parallelization/load balancing, Test Replay, hosted artifacts/history/analytics; paid/premium tiers add richer flake analytics, prioritization/cancellation, UI Coverage, Accessibility, and enterprise controls. [S3][S9][S10][S15][S16][S17][S24]
cost_and_risk.ai_execution_boundary: Deterministic Cypress tests and CI execution do not require an LLM. Studio works without AI or a Cloud account, although current Studio requires internet access; Studio AI and cy.prompt are optional Cloud/AI-assisted authoring or execution features with usage limits and egress. Do not commit cy.prompt into required CI paths if deterministic non-AI operation is a hard requirement. Keep generated assertions under human review, disable Studio AI/guest telemetry where policy requires, and use ordinary explicit cy commands as the complete fallback. Cypress states AI data is session-bound and not used for model training, but use synthetic data and avoid exposing portfolio/customer content regardless. [S20][S23][S24]

evidence_and_decision.confidence: High confidence: release/version, Node 24, TypeScript 6, OS/browser support, license, npm downloads, GitHub stars/forks, core command/network/isolation/artifact behavior, CI guidance, and repository topology, because these come from current official documentation, registry metadata, APIs, and source files. Moderate confidence: application fit, harness burden, ecosystem depth, and weighted score, because they are reasoned from documented behavior without executing Cypress here. Low confidence: issue trend/response distributions, upstream lag duration, maintainer bus factor, comparative rank, and project performance/flake results, because no longitudinal analysis or empirical spike was performed.
evidence_and_decision.hard_gate_result: [uncertain] The project supplied no explicit mandatory-gate list, so the following gates are inferred from fields.yaml. PASS - complete E2E framework. PASS - TypeScript/JavaScript authoring. PASS - Node 24, TypeScript 6, npm, and repository module compatibility. PASS - Linux x64 and GitHub Ubuntu execution. PASS - black-box testing of built Parcel/Gin application without replacing its build. PASS - HTMX/Handlebars dynamic DOM synchronization with disciplined re-querying. PASS - Navigo routes/deep links subject to server fallback. PASS - forms, Chart.js inspection, and downloads. PASS - REST seeding, request observation/mocking, and a custom backend seam for Yahoo Finance. PASS - independent baseUrl/external server. PASS - browser and test-state isolation, with custom PostgreSQL reset. PASS - headless CI, screenshots/video/JUnit, official GitHub Action, and Docker support. PASS - no required paid service. CONDITIONAL PASS - cross-engine coverage because Chrome/Edge/Firefox are stable but WebKit is experimental and native Safari is absent. CONDITIONAL PASS - open-source visual/accessibility workflows require community plugins and project-owned review/reporting. [S1][S2][S3][S9][S10][S13][S16][S17][S18][S21]
evidence_and_decision.deal_breakers: No confirmed project-specific exclusion was found. Potential exclusion conditions are: stable Safari/WebKit coverage is mandatory; native built-in service-free trace/replay and historical flake analytics are mandatory; dynamic sharding must work without Cypress Cloud or custom tooling; native async/await authoring is required; or the team will not accept a framework-specific command queue. None of these constraints is stated as mandatory in the supplied scope. The unperformed spike could still reveal HTMX timing, Gin deep-link, Chart.js, download, or database-reset problems.
evidence_and_decision.project_fit_score: [uncertain] Desk-research score: 85.5/100. Application fit 25/30: strong DOM/network/form/download fit, reduced by non-core accessible locators/visual diffs, custom backend/DB lifecycle, and stale-subject discipline. Maintenance 19/20: current Node/TS/browser support and biweekly releases, reduced by the upcoming v16 transition and experimental WebKit. Reliability 12/15: strong query/action waits, retries, and isolation, reduced by no separate context per test, persistent IndexedDB, and Cloud/custom repeat-history needs. Adoption 14/15: approximately 6.16M weekly npm downloads and 50,983 stars, reduced because registry metrics are not unique E2E projects. CI 8/10: official action/images/caching, reduced by Cloud-gated smart sharding and Compose-in-container complexity. Diagnostics 3.5/5: exceptional local runner plus screenshots/video, reduced by no portable local trace/HAR and Cloud-gated replay. Cost and risk 4/5: MIT core and no required SaaS, reduced by DSL lock-in, binary supply chain, and paid integrated analytics. Score remains uncertain until the same rubric is applied to every candidate and the project spike passes. [S1-S28]
evidence_and_decision.recommendation: [uncertain] Viable alternative. Cypress is strongly maintained, exceptionally adopted, compatible with Node 24 and TypeScript 6, and well suited to this application's HTMX requests, DOM swaps, forms, REST controls, downloads, and GitHub Actions environment. It should advance to an empirical spike. Do not classify it as the final recommended framework before cross-candidate scoring and the spike: experimental WebKit/no native Safari, Cypress-specific queued authoring, lack of per-test browser contexts, and Cloud dependence for first-party smart sharding, replay, and historical flake analytics are material tradeoffs. Prefer Chrome for Testing plus a smaller Firefox matrix, keep Cloud optional, and design DB/Yahoo seams independently of Cypress. [S1][S2][S3][S9][S12][S13][S21][S24]
